Who Helps? Therapists for Autism & ADHD

A GUIDE FOR FAMILIES, EDUCATORS AND ADULTS

The professionals, what each one does, and how they work together.

Welcome. This deck introduces the professionals who support autistic people and people with ADHD: what each discipline focuses on, how care usually unfolds, and what good, respectful support looks like. It is an overview, not medical advice.

Why this matters

1 in 31

11.4%

U.S. 8-year-olds identified as autistic

of U.S. children aged 3–17 have ever been diagnosed with ADHD

Autism and ADHD are common. The CDC's monitoring network found about 1 in 31 eight-year-olds identified as autistic in 2022. About 7 million U.S. children, roughly 11 percent, have ever received an ADHD diagnosis. Many adults are also being identified for the first time. The two often occur together, so families frequently work with several professionals at once.

Autism and ADHD are differences in how a brain is wired, not problems to erase.

The best therapy builds skills, comfort and independence while respecting who the person is.

KEY IDEA

A neurodiversity-affirming approach treats autism and ADHD as natural variations in development. Therapy still matters a great deal: it can ease distress, build communication and daily-living skills, and help people get the accommodations they need. The goal is a better life on the person's own terms, not making someone look typical.

The core therapy team

Occupational therapist (OT)

Speech-language pathologist

Psychologist

Behavior analyst (BCBA)

Diagnostic assessment, therapy for anxiety and mood, parent coaching.

Skill-building plans; choose providers who are play-based and consent-led.

Sensory regulation, motor skills, routines and self-care.

Understanding, expression, social communication and AAC.

Occupational therapists help with sensory processing, handwriting, coordination and daily routines. Speech-language pathologists work on all forms of communication, including augmentative and alternative communication. Psychologists often lead diagnostic evaluations and provide talk therapy such as CBT, plus parent training. Board Certified Behavior Analysts design behavior-based skill programs; practices vary widely, so look for naturalistic, play-based providers who respect the person's assent and avoid compliance-focused drills.

Others who often help

Developmental pediatrician or psychiatrist

Counselor or social worker

ADHD or executive-function coach

Physical therapist

Talk therapy, family support and help finding services.

Strength, balance and coordination when motor skills are a challenge.

Diagnosis, medical care and medication for ADHD or anxiety.

Planning, time and organization skills for teens and adults.

Medical doctors such as developmental-behavioral pediatricians, child psychiatrists and neurologists diagnose, rule out other conditions, and prescribe medication when it helps. Licensed counselors and clinical social workers provide therapy and are often skilled at navigating services. Coaches are not licensed clinicians but can be very practical for planning and follow-through. Physical therapists help with motor delays, low muscle tone or coordination.

How care usually unfolds

Support & review

Parents, teachers or the person spot differences.

A pediatrician or school does a quick check.

Specialists assess strengths and needs.

Goals are set together with the family.

Therapy runs, progress is checked, goals update.

Most journeys start when someone notices a difference. Pediatricians screen for autism at 18 and 24 month checkups and can screen for ADHD from age 4. A full evaluation by a psychologist, developmental pediatrician or team leads to a diagnosis and a picture of strengths and needs. Goals should be written with the family, and with the person themselves whenever possible, then reviewed regularly.

What good care looks like

Look for

Be cautious of

Builds on strengths and interests

Respects every way of communicating

Asks for assent and reads distress

Treats the family as partners

Promises of a cure or recovery

Ignoring signs of distress

One program for every child

No clear goals or progress data

Good therapists are curious about the person, use their interests to motivate learning, accept speech, signs, pictures and devices equally, stop when someone is distressed, and share measurable goals. Be cautious of anyone promising a cure, using expensive unproven treatments, or pushing compliance over comfort and trust.

Key takeaways

Support is a team effort: each discipline covers different needs.

1

Start with a screening or evaluation, then set shared goals.

2

Choose affirming providers who respect the person and the family.

3

Close by reinforcing that there is no single right therapist. Families build a team over time, and needs change with age. Invite questions and point to the other decks in this series for detail on each discipline.
